teaching.hint: After counting occurrences, what is the full possible range of a frequency relative to the input length?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: A frequency is an integer from 1 through n, so it can serve as an index rather than requiring comparison sorting.
solution_outline.approach: Count each value, place values into buckets indexed by their frequency, then scan the buckets from n downward until k values have been collected.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: Every distinct input value belongs to exactly one bucket whose index is its true count; during the descending scan, all collected values have frequency at least that of any later bucket.
solution_outline.correctness: The counting pass assigns every distinct value its exact frequency. Scanning bucket indices from greatest to least collects only values no less frequent than all unscanned values. Once k values are collected, they are exactly the requested top k; arbitrary order within a bucket is permitted.
solution_outline.complexity: Counting, bucket creation, and the bounded bucket scan take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
solution_outline.pitfall: Sorting all distinct values by frequency takes O(n log n), which violates the explicit follow-up requirement.

accepted_alternatives: A selection-based partition around frequencies can achieve expected O(n) time, but requires careful handling of the selection boundary.
common_wrong_turns: Sorting all values instead of their frequency groups
Returning more than k values when a bucket contains a tie
Assuming input values must be nonnegative for a frequency map
source_fidelity_notes: Examples were omitted; arbitrary answer order, uniqueness guarantee, k range, numeric bounds, input size, and stricter-than-O(n-log-n) requirement were retained.
